analysis.one_liner: Tightens Clean Air Act smog rules, cuts car and truck exhaust, and bans leaded gasoline.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a floor vote; after subcommittee hearings in May 1989 it sat in committee, and a year later its substance was carried into H.R. 3030, which became the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the Clean Air Act to fight smog and carbon monoxide in polluted cities. It classified dirty-air areas by severity, required factories to install available pollution controls, pay per-ton fees, and offset new emissions, forced stricter tailpipe standards on new cars, mandated cleaner-burning fleets and vapor-recovery gas nozzles, banned leaded gasoline for road use after 1990, and set deadlines with real penalties for states that missed them. The House committee held hearings but never voted on it; the work was folded into a successor bill that became the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of cities and metro areas with ozone and carbon monoxide pollution, who would breathe cleaner air through tougher factory controls, cleaner vehicles, vapor-recovery at gas pumps, and the end of leaded road gasoline; state and local governments get clearer federal deadlines and backstop sanctions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living in smoggy metro areas

how_it_helps.text: Requires states in polluted areas to submit enforceable plans with interim annual emission-reduction schedules and automatic contingency measures if deadlines are missed.

Applies reasonably available control technology to existing industrial sources, requires offsets for new major sources, and charges sources 25 tons or more per year of emissions for inventory and modeling costs.
Sets stricter tailpipe standards for cars and light trucks built after model year 1992, adds cold-weather carbon monoxide testing, and covers non-road engines, buses, and aircraft.
Prohibits the sale of leaded gasoline for on-road vehicles after 1990 and requires lower sulfur content in diesel fuel.

Requires gas pumps in serious and severe areas to use nozzles that recover hydrocarbon vapors, and gives the EPA authority to sanction states that fail, including construction bans and highway grant cutoffs.

analysis.who_pays: Factories, refineries, and other stationary sources emitting 25 tons or more per year of the targeted pollutants, which face control-technology requirements, offsets, per-ton fees and penalties, and annual permit obligations; automakers facing tighter 1992-and-later emission standards and fleet buyers facing low-emission vehicle quotas; refiners losing leaded gasoline sales and cutting diesel sulfur.

drawbacks.text: Offset requirements of 1.2-to-1 up to 2-to-1 and tighter permit rules would make it more expensive to build or expand factories in nonattainment areas, a real cost to industrial employment in those regions.

Large stationary sources face substantial direct costs: fees for emissions inventories and modeling (initially $25 per ton of nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds), $2,000-per-ton civil penalties in severe areas for missed reductions, and annual compliance permits.

Gasoline stations selling more than 10,000 gallons a month in serious and severe areas must install vapor-recovery fill nozzles, a capital cost, though independent small business marketers get a higher 50,000-gallon threshold.

The bill stretches timelines for the dirtiest areas: severe ozone areas would have until the end of 2005 to meet the standard, and the EPA could grant one-year extensions to moderate and serious areas.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health gains—less smog, less carbon monoxide, no leaded road gasoline, cleaner diesel—are large and broadly shared, while the costs fall on identifiable industries and ultimately show up modestly in prices. The design is fairly conventional for environmental regulation: it ratchets requirements by how badly an area is polluted and builds in deadlines with real sanctions. The main honest criticism is the long runway it gives the worst areas and the compliance burden placed on factories in those areas.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee: it went to two subcommittees, hearings were held in May 1989, and then nothing—on May 23, 1990, the record simply pointed to H.R. 3030, the bill that became the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990.

narrative.text: Representative Al Swift of Washington introduced the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1989 on January 3, 1989, with eight Democratic and one Republican cosponsor; it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee.
On February 6, 1989, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment and the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, which held hearings on May 23 and 24, 1989.
No further action followed; on May 23, 1990, the House action record states 'For Further Action See H.R.3030,' and the bill never received a House floor vote.

The clean air amendments eventually enacted that Congress—the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, signed into law in November 1990—carried substantially the same agenda of smog controls, cleaner vehicles, and an end to leaded gasoline.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people in polluted cities ultimately came out ahead: the substance of this bill became law anyway through H.R. 3030, the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990. For this bill itself, the industries facing its costs benefited from the extra year without new requirements while the successor bill was negotiated.

for.name: Rep. Al Swift
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1989 on January 3, 1989.

for.name: 8 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Mike Synar, Jim Sharp, Dennis Eckart, Jimmy Hayes-era colleagues Slattery, Cooper, Bruce, and Boucher named on the bill.

for.name: 1 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Rep. Billy Tauzin, listed on the introduced bill).

for.name: President George H.W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Sent his own Clean Air Act amendment proposals to Congress in 1989 and pressed for their passage, setting the agenda that the House clean air bills were written to fit.

against.name: John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; it was sent to subcommittees, hearings were held, and the bill was never reported for a floor vote, with the action record later pointing to H.R. 3030.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan but small (8 Democrats and 1 Republican), and the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill bans the sale of leaded gasoline for on-road vehicles after 1990 and requires lower sulfur content in motor vehicle diesel fuel, forcing refiners to change product lines, with a possible two-year delay only if leaded fuel supply for farm vehicles would suffer.

Tighter tailpipe standards for cars and light trucks built after model year 1992, cold-weather testing, expanded anti-tampering rules, and federal fleets required to buy 30 to 90 percent alternative-fuel vehicles cut into the existing product mix and push new technology costs onto manufacturers.

industries.industry: Chemical plants, refineries, and other large stationary polluters
industries.note: Sources emitting 25 tons or more per year of nitrogen oxides or volatile organic compounds face control-technology mandates, 1.2-to-2.0-to-1 emission offsets, annual permits, inventory and modeling fees, and $2,000-per-ton penalties in severe areas—the costs of cleaner air, paid by the emitters.

Stations selling more than 10,000 gallons a month in serious and severe smog areas must install vapor-recovery nozzles, but independent small business marketers get a higher 50,000-gallon threshold, easing the burden on the smallest sellers.

industries.industry: Alternative fuel producers (natural gas, methanol, ethanol)
industries.note: Federal fleets must shift to 30 to 90 percent alternative-fuel vehicles, and fleets of 15 or more cars or light trucks in severe areas face similar mandates, creating a captive early market for cleaner fuels.
